      <description><p>Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds</p><p>One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.</p><p>In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament.       <description><p>A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza</p><p>Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navanethem-navi-pillay-wins-nobel-peace-prize">Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay</a>, if the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/15/myanmar-rohingya-genocide-icj">court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide</a> against the Rohingya.</p><p>The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/18/us-sanctions-icj-judges-myanmar-genocide-ruling-israel-gaza-court">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/16/eu-states-immigration-return-hubs-rwanda</link>
      <description><p>Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’</p><p>Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.</p><p>The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/mar/26/meps-back-plans-for-return-hubs-raising-fears-of-human-rights-black-holes">newly agreed returns law</a> that allows<em> </em>people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/16/eu-states-immigration-return-hubs-rwanda">Continue reading...</a></description>

The Voyager 1 probe launched by NASA nearly a half century ago has reached a distance from Earth of one light day (more than 26 billion kilometres), the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from our planet. The space agency received a signal from the spacecraft Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/667c80bc-e444-11f1-afff-13439ca2fe89/w:1024/p:16x9/AP24166764529324.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/667c80bc-e444-11f1-afff-13439ca2fe89/w:1024/p:16x9/AP24166764529324.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">8ce9cafc-e444-11f1-9311-c9f272e956c0</guid><pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:26:18 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/667c80bc-e444-11f1-afff-13439ca2fe89/w:1024/p:16x9/AP24166764529324.jpg">© NASA via AP (file image)</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>France</category><title>French media regulator says it will monitor top YouTubers for bias in election coverage</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261119-french-regulator-warns-influential-youtubers-respect-pluralism-rules-election-coverage</link><description>
Rules designed to safeguard media pluralism during elections campaigns will apply to France's most influential YouTubers in the run-up to next year's presidential contest, media regulator Arcom warned on Thursday, reflecting the growing influence of content creators whose audiences often outstrip those of traditional media companies.

Despite warm words between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen Thursday, the simmering trade war between Washington and Beijing still looks to be no closer to resolution.

Hundreds of supporters of ousted Bangladesh premier Sheikh Hasina staged street protests on Thursday, as a wave of arson attacks escalated tensions ahead of her planned return from exile next month. 
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5276727a-e43b-11f1-a52f-13439ca2fe89/w:1024/p:16x9/Bangladesh-protests-Hasina0.png"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5276727a-e43b-11f1-a52f-13439ca2fe89/w:1024/p:16x9/Bangladesh-protests-Hasina0.png" type="image/png" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">86c1ef50-e43b-11f1-a5c4-cbf5d8d01bb9</guid><pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:14:23 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Tête à tête</category><title>US has 'unbalanced approach' on DR Congo deal, Rwanda's foreign minister says</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/t%C3%AAte-%C3%A0-t%C3%AAte/20261119-us-has-unbalanced-approach-on-dr-congo-deal-rwanda-s-foreign-minister-says</link><description>
In an interview with FRANCE 24, Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe said the Trump administration had "an unbalanced approach" in implementing the DR Congo peace deal it brokered. Finally, he defended a deal for Rwanda to host failed asylum seekers from five European countries.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1da1c348-e417-11f1-91e2-1bac47ab2f5d/w:1024/p:16x9/FR-NW-PKG-CLEAN-EN-TETE-A-TETE-Olivier-J-P-Nduhungirehe-AUBIN-Sophian.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/1da1c348-e417-11f1-91e2-1bac47ab2f5d/w:1024/p:16x9/FR-NW-PKG-CLEAN-EN-TETE-A-TETE-Olivier-J-P-Nduhungirehe-AUBIN-Sophian.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">3e342fd8-e42b-11f1-8816-c724df93fed8</guid><pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:07:09 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Marc PERELMAN</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

China's space station is set to receive its first foreign astronaut.

A Long March 2F rocket, topped with the Shenzhou-24 crew spacecraft, was rolled out to the pad at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, on Tuesday (Nov. 17), with launch expected in the next week.

The 191-foot-tall (58 meters) rocket was transferred 0.93 miles (1.5 kilometers) from a vertical integration building to the pad over the course of around two hours, starting around 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT, or 5 p.m. Beijing Time), according to China Central Television (CCTV).

China's human spaceflight agency, CMSA, stated that all facilities and equipment at the launch site are in good condition, adding that the launch is scheduled to take place in the coming days, without providing a date.

CMSA typically holds a press conference at Jiuquan a day ahead of launch, during which the crew for the mission is revealed to the public. This time, one of the three crew members will, for the first time, be an international astronaut. One of two Pakistani astronaut candidates will fly to the Tiangong space station on Shenzhou-24, marking a first both for China's outpost and for Pakistan, which will see one its astronauts reach orbit for the first time.

Though public details are sparse, it is thought that the Pakistani astronaut, operating as a payload specialist, will stay aboard Tiangong for around a week, returning home on the departing Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

One of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts — who are approaching the end of their six-month-long mission, having launched on May 24 — will stay aboard Tiangong for another half a year. This will provide the international visitor with a seat home on Shenzhou-23, and allow a Chinese astronaut to make the country's first year-long stay in orbit. This extra-long mission will supply China with data on physiology ahead of crewed lunar flights and other long-duration missions.

China approved its human spaceflight program in 1992 and launched its first orbital crewed mission in 2003, with Yang Liwei becoming the first Chinese national in space. The country then completed the three-module Tiangong space station in late 2022 and has kept the orbital outpost constantly crewed ever since, with rotating six-month-long missions with brief handovers between crews.

Shenzhou-24 will be China's 18th crewed mission and will mark the first time a foreign national is flying on a Shenzhou spacecraft. China is also looking to double the size of Tiangong in the coming years, potentially opening the way to further international missions and space tourist visits.

The Empire State Building glowed in glittering gold last night (Nov. 17) to celebrate NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hitting one light-day from Earth. And it isn't the only building celebrating this achievement with a sparkling display.

What is it?

Today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe. So any signal we send to Voyager 1 or it sends back now takes a full day as the spacecraft continues to explore interstellar space.

To celebrate the major milestone for the farthest human-made object in history, the Empire State Building in New York City lit up in gold. This golden glow references the Golden Record onboard both the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft.

And the Empire State Building wasn't the only major landmark to celebrate the occasion. The Space Needle in Seattle, Washington, and both the Willis Tower and the Skydeck Chicago in Chicago, Illinois have all been illuminated gold to mark the milestone.

Why is it incredible?

The Golden Record that these gold glowing buildings are referencing serves as an inanimate ambassador for Earth, carrying information about humanity, our planet, the other species who live here, the languages we speak, the music we listen to and so much more. It even includes instructions for building a record player to play the record.

The Voyager mission has, and continues to, make incredible scientific discoveries and observations throughout our solar system and now in interstellar space. But this Golden Record provides an additional aspect to the mission that connects us here on Earth to whatever unknown life may exist out there.

If some sort of life forms out in the cosmos were to ever come across Voyager and its Golden Record at any point in the distant future, they might learn a little bit about our small blue dot.

]]> <![CDATA[ Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video) ]]> The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.

The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off.

Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature.

But back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display.

Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two.

"I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email.

"My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows."

Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds.

Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X.

"Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X.

This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively quickly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine.

Meanwhile, over Deming, New Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak.

"While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email.

"But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog."

But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky.

"One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued.

Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens.

And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America.

In Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19.

The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky.

A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies.

Elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture.

But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest.

Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures.

The Leonids were already making an appearance in the days leading up to the shower's peak.

On Nov. 16, astrophotographer @EricTheSpaceCat captured several possible Leonids streaking through the sky.

If the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids, one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness.

]]> <![CDATA[ Nonprofit Common Space will launch 1st 'humanitarian satellite' in 2027 ]]> The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan.

The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites, whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.

That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites: Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company.

There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space.

The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it says will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery.

Satellogic is now officially part of this picture.

"With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come."

The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process.

The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth. But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm).

The satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully.

And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the company stressed.

"Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happening so they can act with confidence," Luciano Giesso, vice president of space systems at Satellogic, said in the same statement. "This mission puts our vision of democratized access into practice."

Common Space is currently raising money to expand the constellation to six satellites, which it hopes to have in place by 2030. This will allow daily high-resolution coverage of "priority areas," according to the nonprofit.

Editor's note: The original version of this story stated that the first Satellogic satellite will launch on a SpaceX rocket. This information was in an embargoed version of today's press release but was not in the final version, so it has been removed from this story.

As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect."

In the new study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

In 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

Then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar said.

In the new study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar said.

Although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar said. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down."

Now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar said. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events."

The scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

      <title>Školní autobus se střetl s autem. Řidička je mrtvá, zraněné děti vytahovali okénkem</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/plzen/zpravy/nehoda-autobus-auto-kaznejov-tremosna-zraneni.A261119_110903_plzen-zpravy_epkbn#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Tragicky skončila dopolední čelní srážka autobusu s předškolními dětmi, které jely z divadelního představení, a osobního auta na severním Plzeňsku mezi Třemošnou a Kaznějovem. Řidička osobního auta zemřela. Dalších čtrnáct zraněných, z toho deset dětí, odvezli záchranáři do nemocnic, žádný z nich nemá vážné zranění. Tah z Plzně na Most byl hodiny uzavřený.</description>

      <guid isPermaLink="false">A261119_110903_plzen-zpravy_epkbn</guid>
      <media:content url="https://1gr.cz/fotky/idnes/26/112/cl6/PKZ68ab3fb4d7_IMG_4810_kopie.JPG" type="image/jpeg" />
      <media:description>Z havarovaného autobusu záchranáři převezli do nemocnice deset dětí a tři dospělé. Jejich zranění nejsou vážná. Řidička osobního vozu, která se s autobusem střetla, ale nehodu nepřežila.</media:description>

 <description>Koalice ochotných bude i v celém příštím roce Ukrajinu podporovat. Po jednání více než čtyř desítek členů koalice v Berlíně to řekl německý kancléř Friedrich Merz. Ruského prezidenta Vladimira Putina vyzval, aby válku proti Ukrajině ukončil a začal jednat o míru.  <description>Mezinárodní soudní dvůr (ICJ) ve čtvrtek rozhodl, že tisíce vražd a rozsáhlé sexuální násilí, kterých se v roce 2017 dopustily bezpečnostní složky v Barmě na příslušnících skupiny Rohingů, představují genocidu podporovanou státem. Soudní dvůr uvedl, že záměrem Barmy tehdy bylo zničit významnou část příslušníků této muslimské menšiny. Je to poprvé, kdy nejvyšší soud OSN shledal nějaký stát odpovědným za genocidu.</description>

 <description>Ministr životního prostředí Igor Červený (Motoristé sobě) se vypravil na svou první klimatickou konferenci OSN v Turecku. V národním projevu označil za českou prioritu adaptaci na změnu klimatu a mluvil o rizicích dekarbonizace. V rozhovoru pro iROZHLAS.cz označuje snahu o odklon od fosilních paliv za náboženství a uklidňuje tichomořské národy ohrožené stoupáním oceánů.  <description>Princ Harry se aktivně angažuje v pomoci válečným veteránům, jedním z nichž se sám v roce 2015 stal.  <description>V čínském Šen-čenu se ve čtvrtek sešli prezidenti Číny, USA a Ruska Si Ťin-pching, Donald Trump a Vladimir Putin.  <description>Na Krymském mostě byl po dalším ukrajinském útoku přerušen provoz vlaků, oznámilo ve čtvrtek podle ruské služby BBC ministerstvo dopravy v Moskvě. Kyjev aktuální úder potvrdil. Ukrajina na most, který přes Kerčský průliv spojuje ruskou pevninu s Krymem, zaútočila již v úterý a vážně ho poškodila. Po úterním úderu na něm byla zastavena automobilová doprava.</description>

 <title>Konečně je sečteno, demokraté získají v Senátu 56 křesel. Ve sněmovně hledají na Trumpa ‚ostříleného právníka‘</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/konecne-je-secteno-demokrate-ziskaji-v-senatu-56-kresel-ve-snemovne-hledaji-na_2611190500_vdv</link>
 <description>Dva týdny po amerických volbách jsou známy výsledky z Aljašky, kde Demokratická strana získala 56. křeslo v Senátu a v horní komoře Kongresu má nejsilnější mandát od roku 1958. Dalším krokem pro demokraty je zvolit si vedení, které příští dva roky povede opozici vůči Bílému domu. Stávající předseda Chuck Schumer tvrdí, že už teď má mezi spolustraníky dost hlasů. Prosincová volba předsedy však bude tajná a Schumer je nepopulární.</description>

</item>
<item>
 <title>Deportační centrum ve Rwandě? Unijní státy se vrhají do slepé uličky jako Británie, míní Magda Faltová</title>
 <link>https://www.irozhlas.cz/zpravy-svet/deportacni-centrum-ve-rwande-unijni-staty-se-vrhaji-do-slepe-ulicky-jako_2611190010_cen</link>
 <description>Pět evropských zemí chce neúspěšné žadatele o azyl posílat do Rwandy. Jaký efekt může přinést zřízení deportačního centra v této africké zemi? Může fungovat jako odstrašení příchozích? „Státy o tom často mluví, ale čísla, data a výzkumy to nepotvrzují,“ říká pro Radiožurnál Magda Faltová, ředitelka Sdružení pro integraci a migraci. Co zavádí přísnější migrační politika EU? A měla by být tvrdší také pravidla pro slučování rodin uprchlíků?</description>
